questions.stem: Which finding is required to classify a fracture as open?

choices.text: A skin wound anywhere on the injured extremity
choices.explanation: The wound must communicate with the fracture.

choices.text: A wound communicating with the fracture
choices.explanation: Communication with the fracture defines an open fracture.

choices.text: A wound with bone visibly protruding through the skin
choices.explanation: Visible bone is not required for a fracture to be open.

choices.text: A fracture with severe surrounding bruising and swelling
choices.explanation: Bruising and swelling alone do not establish communication with the outside.

questions.point: An open fracture communicates with an external wound; visible bone is not required.

questions.stem: Which assessment set most directly checks for immediate limb and systemic complications after an open fracture?

choices.text: Joint range, walking distance, muscle bulk and rehabilitation goals
choices.explanation: Rehabilitation measures do not replace assessment for immediate complications.

choices.text: Wound dimensions, dressing type, exudate volume and skin edges
choices.explanation: This wound-focused set omits distal function and systemic observations.

choices.text: Pain score, sleep quality, appetite and response to reassurance
choices.explanation: These do not adequately check perfusion, movement and systemic stability.

choices.text: Bleeding, distal perfusion, sensation, movement and vital signs
choices.explanation: These identify bleeding, neurovascular change and systemic deterioration.

questions.point: Open-fracture nursing assessment includes bleeding, wound, distal neurovascular status, pain/swelling and vitals.

questions.stem: Which infection-prevention plan fits nursing care for a fresh open fracture?

choices.text: Protect aseptically; await visible drainage before ordered antibiotics
choices.explanation: The infection-prevention plan should not wait for drainage to appear.

choices.text: Clean the surface; omit antibiotics if bone is not visible
choices.explanation: Visible protruding bone is not required for an open fracture.

choices.text: Protect aseptically; give ordered antibiotics; verify tetanus assessment
choices.explanation: These match the taught plan while preserving authorized prescribing.

choices.text: Cover the wound; omit tetanus assessment after starting antibiotics
choices.explanation: Antibiotics do not replace tetanus assessment.

questions.point: Protect the wound, follow the ordered antimicrobial plan, verify tetanus assessment and avoid independent wound manipulation.

questions.stem: An open-fracture wound develops increasing pain, redness, swelling and purulent drainage. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: This pattern proves normal fracture healing
choices.explanation: Purulent drainage and worsening inflammation are not normal healing findings.

choices.text: The findings can be ignored if hardware is intact
choices.explanation: Hardware appearance does not exclude infection.

choices.text: Only fever can indicate infection
choices.explanation: Local infection can be evident before prominent systemic signs.

choices.text: These are infection warning signs that require review
choices.explanation: The pattern is consistent with worsening wound infection.

questions.point: Increasing pain, redness, swelling, purulent drainage or fever are infection warning signs.

questions.stem: A patient with an open leg fracture develops worsening sensation and movement in the foot. What is the priority?

choices.text: Wait for the next routine dressing change
choices.explanation: This delays assessment of possible limb compromise.

choices.text: Urgent neurovascular reassessment and escalation
choices.explanation: Deteriorating nerve or perfusion findings can threaten the limb.

choices.text: Assume swelling alone explains all neurological changes
choices.explanation: New neurological loss requires urgent review.

choices.text: Document the finding without contacting the team
choices.explanation: Documentation does not replace escalation.

questions.point: Neurovascular deterioration or systemic deterioration after an open fracture requires urgent escalation.

exams.feedback: show keys and all option explanations after submission
exams.retestPolicy: same standard form after required reading

questions.stem: What is the key anatomical difference between BKA and AKA?

choices.text: BKA preserves the ankle; AKA removes below the ankle
choices.explanation: BKA removes the distal leg and foot, including the ankle.

choices.text: BKA preserves the knee; AKA removes the limb above it
choices.explanation: The knee is retained in BKA but not AKA.

choices.text: BKA removes the knee; AKA preserves the knee joint
choices.explanation: This reverses the relationship.

choices.text: BKA removes above the hip; AKA removes below it
choices.explanation: These terms use the knee, not the hip, as the distinction.

questions.point: BKA preserves the knee, whereas AKA is above the knee and generally requires more energy for mobility.

questions.stem: Which focused sequence is most appropriate after lower-limb amputation?

choices.text: Only phantom sensation
choices.explanation: Phantom pain matters but is not the entire assessment.

choices.text: Diet preference, sleep pattern, then wound appearance
choices.explanation: This omits immediate postoperative risks.

choices.text: Only prosthetic fit on the first postoperative assessment
choices.explanation: Early care prioritizes bleeding, wound, circulation and pain.

choices.text: Bleeding, wound/infection, residual-limb circulation, pain and position
choices.explanation: These are the high-yield postoperative nursing priorities taught.

questions.point: Post-amputation nursing assessment prioritizes bleeding, wound/infection, residual-limb circulation, pain and position.

questions.stem: Which description defines phantom limb pain?

choices.text: Pain perceived in the part of the limb that was removed
choices.explanation: Phantom limb pain is real pain perceived in the missing part.

choices.text: A painless sense that the missing limb is still present
choices.explanation: This describes phantom sensation without pain.

choices.text: Pain confined to the skin around the residual-limb incision
choices.explanation: This describes residual-limb pain rather than phantom pain.

choices.text: Pain caused by pressure where a prosthesis contacts the limb
choices.explanation: This is pain at the remaining limb’s contact site.

questions.point: Phantom limb pain is real pain perceived in the removed limb.

questions.stem: Why should prolonged flexion of a residual limb be avoided?

choices.text: Risk of wound bleeding from any return to extension
choices.explanation: This is not the contracture-prevention rationale; follow the individual positioning plan.

choices.text: Risk of distal bone infection from extending the joint
choices.explanation: This does not explain the positioning precaution.

choices.text: Risk of recurrent phantom pain with each joint extension
choices.explanation: Phantom pain is not the reason prolonged flexion is avoided.

choices.text: Risk of flexion contracture and reduced joint range
choices.explanation: Prolonged flexion can limit extension and later function.

questions.point: Avoid prolonged flexion because it can promote flexion contracture; follow the positioning and physiotherapy plan.

questions.stem: A post-amputation dressing becomes rapidly blood-soaked and the patient becomes tachycardic. What is the priority?

choices.text: Wait for the next scheduled dressing round
choices.explanation: Possible hemorrhage requires prompt action.

choices.text: Focus first on phantom pain education
choices.explanation: Bleeding takes priority.

choices.text: Assess circulation/vitals and escalate urgently for possible hemorrhage
choices.explanation: Rapid bleeding with tachycardia can indicate significant blood loss.

choices.text: Encourage independent walking before assessment
choices.explanation: Mobilization is unsafe before evaluating possible hemorrhage.

questions.point: Active or increasing bleeding after amputation requires urgent assessment and escalation.

exams.title: Orthopaedic Pain + Common Medications

timing.timerEnforcement: persisted total deadline: 90 seconds multiplied by question count

scoring.criticalSafetyMiss: separate follow-up required; original numeric score unchanged

exams.feedback: show keys and all option explanations after submission
exams.retestPolicy: same standard form after required reading

questions.stem: Why should pain be reassessed as a trend rather than treated as a number alone?

choices.text: Unexpectedly worsening pain can signal a new limb complication
choices.explanation: Pain trend can reveal deterioration such as neurovascular compromise or infection.

choices.text: Only the first pain score is clinically useful
choices.explanation: Response and change over time matter.

choices.text: Pain severity always identifies the exact diagnosis
choices.explanation: Pain alone is not diagnostic.

choices.text: A lower score means neurovascular checks are unnecessary
choices.explanation: Other limb findings still matter.

questions.point: Unexpectedly worsening orthopaedic pain should trigger reassessment for a cause, not just repeated analgesia.

questions.stem: Which medication-safety pairing is correct?

choices.text: Gabapentin: it cannot contribute to drowsiness
choices.explanation: Gabapentin can cause drowsiness and ataxia.

choices.text: Tramadol: respiratory status never matters
choices.explanation: Sedation and respiratory depression can occur.

choices.text: Ketorolac: combine freely with other NSAIDs
choices.explanation: Duplicate NSAIDs increase adverse-effect risk.

choices.text: Paracetamol: count the total from all products
choices.explanation: Duplicate acetaminophen/paracetamol can create overdose risk.

questions.point: Common IBD2 analgesics require product-specific safety checks: total paracetamol, no duplicate NSAIDs, and sedation/respiratory monitoring for sedating drugs.

questions.stem: After a sedating analgesic, which assessment set best checks both benefit and immediate adverse effects?

choices.text: Pain response, bowel sounds and appetite
choices.explanation: These do not adequately assess immediate sedation and breathing.

choices.text: Pain response, joint range and walking distance
choices.explanation: Functional measures do not replace checking alertness and breathing.

choices.text: Pain response, alertness and respiratory pattern
choices.explanation: This checks analgesic effect and sedation-related respiratory compromise.

choices.text: Pain response, wound dimensions and drainage
choices.explanation: These wound findings do not establish respiratory safety.

questions.point: After analgesia, reassess pain response and monitor alertness/respiration when sedating medicines are used.

questions.stem: A fracture patient reports severe pain that is much worse than expected and passive stretch increases it. What should come before simply giving more analgesia?

choices.text: Wait until the pain score reaches 10/10
choices.explanation: Urgency is not defined by one numerical threshold.

choices.text: Assume tolerance to pain medicine has developed
choices.explanation: This can miss limb-threatening deterioration.

choices.text: Encourage weight-bearing to test the limb
choices.explanation: This is unsafe in a potentially compromised limb.

choices.text: Repeat the neurovascular assessment and escalate concern
choices.explanation: The pain pattern can warn of acute compartment syndrome.

questions.point: Danger pain requires limb and neurovascular reassessment before assuming the problem is inadequate analgesia.

questions.stem: Which source should guide a check of a prescribed analgesic’s route and interactions?

choices.text: A previous patient’s regimen for the same pain score
choices.explanation: A prior regimen is not a substitute for checking this prescription.

choices.text: The trade name without checking the active ingredient
choices.explanation: The ingredient and formulation must be identified.

choices.text: Current drug/product information matched to the prescription
choices.explanation: Administration and interactions depend on the specific drug and product.

choices.text: The general pain lesson applied to every analgesic
choices.explanation: The general lesson cannot supply every product-specific administration detail.

questions.point: Use the verified medication entry and current order for drug-specific administration, contraindications and interactions.

timing.timerEnforcement: persisted total deadline: 90 seconds multiplied by question count

scoring.criticalSafetyMiss: separate follow-up required; original numeric score unchanged

exams.feedback: show keys and all option explanations after submission

questions.stem: What should be verified before mobilizing an orthopaedic patient?

choices.text: Pain score, preferred route and planned walking distance
choices.explanation: These do not establish the permitted loading or required support.

choices.text: Previous activity level, shoe size and exercise preference
choices.explanation: Baseline details do not replace current postoperative orders.

choices.text: Weight-bearing order, mobility aid and required assistance
choices.explanation: These establish how the patient can mobilize under the individual plan.

choices.text: Frame appearance, patient confidence and available corridor space
choices.explanation: Appearance and confidence do not establish a safe authorized mobility plan.

questions.point: Before mobilizing, verify prescribed weight-bearing status, assistive device and needed assistance.

questions.stem: Which pair of pressure areas is particularly important in a patient lying supine for prolonged periods?

choices.text: Sacrum and heels
choices.explanation: These are major pressure-bearing areas in this position.

choices.text: Palms and anterior elbows
choices.explanation: These are not the main pressure-bearing areas in supine lying.

choices.text: Ears and lateral ankles
choices.explanation: These are more relevant to lateral contact in side lying.

choices.text: Cheeks and anterior knees
choices.explanation: These are more relevant to anterior contact in prone positioning.

questions.point: Immobility requires skin inspection and repositioning/weight shifts, especially at high-risk pressure areas such as sacrum and heels.

questions.stem: Which new limb pattern most strongly suggests DVT?

choices.text: Symmetric ankle swelling after prolonged dependent sitting
choices.explanation: This is less specific for a new unilateral venous thrombosis.

choices.text: Focal redness exactly beneath a tight dressing edge
choices.explanation: This suggests local contact pressure rather than the described calf pattern.

choices.text: Chronic knee stiffness that improves after gentle movement
choices.explanation: This does not fit the new calf swelling and warmth pattern.

choices.text: New unilateral calf swelling, tenderness and warmth
choices.explanation: This cluster raises concern for DVT and requires assessment.

questions.point: New unilateral swelling, pain, warmth or redness should raise concern for DVT.

questions.stem: An immobilized patient suddenly develops dyspnea and chest pain. What is the priority?

choices.text: Massage the painful calf vigorously
choices.explanation: Manipulation is not an appropriate response to suspected DVT/PE.

choices.text: Wait for routine physiotherapy review
choices.explanation: This delays emergency assessment.

choices.text: Urgent escalation for possible pulmonary embolism while assessing ABCs/vitals
choices.explanation: PE is a medical emergency.

choices.text: Encourage unassisted walking to improve circulation
choices.explanation: This is unsafe during possible PE.

questions.point: Sudden dyspnea/chest pain in a VTE-risk patient requires emergency escalation for possible PE.

questions.stem: Which prevention approach best matches the taught VTE plan after fracture repair?

choices.text: Use compression even when specifically contraindicated
choices.explanation: Patient-specific orders and contraindications matter.

choices.text: Start anticoagulation independently without an order
choices.explanation: Anticoagulants require the authorized plan.

choices.text: Keep every patient on strict bed rest regardless of orders
choices.explanation: Unnecessary immobility increases complications.

choices.text: Mobilize when allowed and follow prescribed anticoagulation/compression
choices.explanation: These are established prevention measures when appropriate.

questions.point: VTE prevention may include early mobilization when allowed plus prescribed anticoagulation and compression.

choices.explanation: This connects the leg findings with the sudden respiratory symptoms.

choices.text: Joint stiffness associated with reduced physical activity
choices.explanation: Joint stiffness does not explain the new calf and respiratory findings.

choices.text: Local wound infection with pain-limited chest expansion
choices.explanation: This does not explain the combined pattern as well as possible thromboembolism.

choices.text: Pressure injury associated with prolonged immobilization
choices.explanation: A pressure injury does not explain the sudden cardiopulmonary change.

questions.point: Sudden dyspnea/chest pain in a VTE-risk patient requires emergency escalation for possible PE.

questions.stem: Which prevention approach best matches the taught VTE plan after fracture repair?

choices.text: Use compression even when specifically contraindicated
choices.explanation: Patient-specific orders and contraindications matter.

choices.text: Start anticoagulation independently without an order
choices.explanation: Anticoagulants require the authorized plan.

choices.text: Mobilize when allowed and follow prescribed anticoagulation/compression
choices.explanation: These are established prevention measures when appropriate.

choices.text: Keep every patient on strict bed rest regardless of orders
choices.explanation: Unnecessary immobility increases complications.

questions.point: VTE prevention may include early mobilization when allowed plus prescribed anticoagulation and compression.

questions.stem: What does an elevated CRP tell you by itself?

choices.text: A bacterial cause rather than a noninfectious inflammatory cause
choices.explanation: CRP alone cannot distinguish these causes.

choices.text: A susceptible organism rather than an antibiotic-resistant organism
choices.explanation: CRP does not identify an organism or its susceptibility.

choices.text: Bone involvement rather than infection limited to soft tissue
choices.explanation: CRP does not locate the inflammation.

choices.text: An inflammatory response without identifying its cause
choices.explanation: CRP is nonspecific; interpret it with the clinical findings.

questions.point: CRP is a nonspecific inflammatory marker and must be interpreted with the clinical picture and trend.

questions.stem: Which mapping correctly links CBC components with their main assessment context?

choices.text: WBC: bleeding; hemoglobin: infection; platelets: anemia
choices.explanation: These are not the correct component-to-context relationships.

choices.text: WBC: anemia; hemoglobin: bleeding; platelets: infection
choices.explanation: This misassigns the main assessment role of WBC and platelets.

choices.text: WBC: infection; hemoglobin: anemia; platelets: bleeding
choices.explanation: These components support these respective assessment contexts.

choices.text: WBC: infection; hemoglobin: clotting; platelets: anemia
choices.explanation: Hemoglobin assesses anemia; platelets relate to bleeding and clotting.

questions.point: CBC components support infection, anemia/blood-loss and bleeding-risk assessment.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a correctly collected culture?

choices.text: Identify an organism to help guide antimicrobial treatment
choices.explanation: Culture supports organism identification and treatment selection.

choices.text: Establish the depth of bone involvement from the specimen alone
choices.explanation: Culture alone does not establish anatomical extent.

choices.text: Measure circulating white cells to assess infection severity
choices.explanation: A CBC measures circulating cells; culture has a different purpose.

choices.text: Measure the inflammatory response to compare with CRP
choices.explanation: Culture investigates organisms, not the magnitude of inflammation.

questions.point: A correctly collected culture helps identify the organism and guide antimicrobial therapy.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected fracture-related infection is unstable and septic. Cultures have not yet been collected. What is the safest principle?

choices.text: Ignore cultures permanently once treatment begins
choices.explanation: Sampling can still be important when clinically feasible.

choices.text: Withhold all treatment until every specimen is collected
choices.explanation: This can dangerously delay care.

choices.text: Do not delay urgent treatment solely to obtain cultures
choices.explanation: Sepsis requires immediate assessment and treatment.

choices.text: Use CRP alone to choose the antibiotic
choices.explanation: CRP does not identify the organism.

questions.point: In an unstable septic patient, urgent treatment must not be delayed solely for culture collection.

questions.stem: CRP and ESR remain elevated, but the wound and patient are clinically improving. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: Interpret marker trends alongside the improving clinical findings
choices.explanation: CRP and ESR are nonspecific and must be interpreted with the clinical course.

choices.text: Interpret clinical improvement as evidence that infection is eradicated
choices.explanation: Improvement alone does not prove complete eradication.

choices.text: Interpret persistent elevation as evidence that treatment has failed
choices.explanation: An elevated marker alone does not establish treatment failure.

choices.text: Interpret the marker values as more decisive than the wound findings
choices.explanation: Markers do not replace the overall clinical assessment.

questions.point: Inflammatory markers support assessment but do not diagnose or define worsening osteomyelitis by themselves.

timing.timerEnforcement: persisted total deadline: 90 seconds multiplied by question count

questions.stem: What does the A in SBAR represent?

choices.text: Assessment
choices.explanation: A contains focused findings and the nurse’s evaluation.

choices.text: Allergies
choices.explanation: Allergies are relevant background, not the meaning of A.

choices.text: Admission
choices.explanation: Admission history belongs in relevant background, not the A heading.

choices.text: Action
choices.explanation: Actions may be reported, but the A heading means Assessment.

questions.point: SBAR means Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation/Request.

questions.stem: After escalation of deterioration, which chart entry best allows the next nurse to judge the response?

choices.text: Timed findings, actions, instructions and routine medication list
choices.explanation: The medication list does not show whether the patient improved.

choices.text: Timed findings, actions, instructions and repeat observations
choices.explanation: These link the change and response to the care given.

choices.text: Timed findings, actions, instructions and planned appointments
choices.explanation: Planned appointments do not show the response to the intervention.

choices.text: Timed findings, actions, instructions and prior medical history
choices.explanation: Relevant background does not substitute for observations after the intervention.

questions.point: Document time, objective findings, action, notification, instructions and the patient's response/reassessment.

questions.stem: Why is read-back used for new verbal or telephone orders?

choices.text: Confirm the order matches the previous patient’s regimen
choices.explanation: Orders must be checked for this patient, not matched to another patient.

choices.text: Confirm the treatment produced the intended clinical response
choices.explanation: Reassessment, rather than read-back, establishes treatment response.

choices.text: Confirm the receiving nurse has completed the intervention
choices.explanation: Read-back verifies the message before it is carried out.

choices.text: Confirm the order matches what the prescriber intended
choices.explanation: Read-back detects misheard or misunderstood instructions.

questions.point: New verbal/telephone orders should be repeated back according to policy and documented.

questions.stem: A patient with an external fixator develops fever, worse pain and purulent drainage. Which statement belongs in Situation?

choices.text: The external fixator was inserted after an open fracture
choices.explanation: This is relevant Background rather than the new problem.

choices.text: New fever, increased pain and purulent drainage prompted this call
choices.explanation: Situation states the current problem requiring attention.

choices.text: Please review the patient and advise on the treatment plan
choices.explanation: This states a Recommendation or request.

choices.text: I am concerned about an infection involving the pin site
choices.explanation: This is the nurse’s Assessment of the problem.

questions.point: A useful SBAR begins with the current change, then relevant background, focused assessment and a clear request.

questions.stem: Which escalation note leaves the response to a new sensory deficit unclear?

choices.text: New toe numbness at 14:00; urgent review; instructions and repeat findings recorded
choices.explanation: This records the response and follow-up.

choices.text: New toe numbness at 14:00; review completed; plan and subsequent sensation recorded
choices.explanation: This allows comparison after the response.

choices.text: New toe numbness at 14:00; team attended; instructions and repeat movement recorded
choices.explanation: This includes the received plan and reassessment.

choices.text: New toe numbness at 14:00; doctor notified; review requested
choices.explanation: The note lacks instructions received and subsequent reassessment.

questions.point: Avoid vague documentation such as “doctor informed” without the clinical details and follow-up.

questions.stem: A fracture patient has severe increasing pain on passive stretch and tingling, but a pulse is present. What is the priority?

choices.text: Give analgesia and end the assessment
choices.explanation: Pain relief must not replace emergency assessment.

choices.text: Encourage walking to test the limb
choices.explanation: This is unsafe.

choices.text: Urgent neurovascular reassessment and escalation for compartment syndrome
choices.explanation: A pulse does not exclude acute compartment syndrome.

choices.text: Wait until the pulse disappears
choices.explanation: Pulselessness is a late finding.

questions.point: Recognize compartment syndrome despite a palpable pulse and escalate urgently.

questions.stem: An external fixator has purulent drainage and a component appears loose. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Ignore the drainage if the pulse is present
choices.explanation: A pulse does not exclude infection or hardware problems.

choices.text: Assess the patient/limb, protect it and escalate without adjusting the frame
choices.explanation: Both infection and mechanical problems require authorized review.

choices.text: Tighten the frame before checking the patient
choices.explanation: Independent adjustment can alter alignment.

choices.text: Allow unrestricted walking to test stability
choices.explanation: This is unsafe.

questions.point: External-fixator infection or hardware problems require assessment, protection and escalation without independent adjustment.

questions.stem: A post-BKA dressing rapidly soaks with blood and the heart rate rises. What is the priority?

choices.text: Focus on phantom pain first
choices.explanation: Hemorrhage takes priority.

choices.text: Wait for the next scheduled dressing change
choices.explanation: This delays urgent care.

choices.text: Begin routine gait training
choices.explanation: Mobility is not the immediate priority.

choices.text: Assess circulation/vitals and escalate for possible hemorrhage
choices.explanation: Bleeding with tachycardia is a postoperative emergency concern.

questions.point: Rapid postoperative bleeding after amputation requires urgent hemorrhage assessment and escalation.
